Nose-touch avoidance shows a striking degree of conservation: five of the six species we tested showed the behavior (Figure 5A). Transduction is the process by which physical and chemical signals are converted into neural impulses, the mechanism that makes it possible to perceive the world at all. In the nervous system, transduction refers to the translation of stimuli into electrical signals. In sensory transduction specifically, physical or chemical inputs are transformed by specialized sensory receptors into electrical impulses that travel to the brain.

The visual system offers a clear example. Within the retina, rod and cone cells serve as the bridge between the physical environment and neural communication. When light strikes these photoreceptors, it triggers a conformational change in the protein rhodopsin. That molecular shift sets off a cascade of events that alters the photoreceptor's electrochemical gradient. As the gradient decreases, so do the electrical signals sent to the brain. In other words, more light hitting the photoreceptor results in fewer electrical impulses, a counterintuitive arrangement but one that allows the brain to decode the visual world with great precision.

**Mobile Gaming: The Next Evolution of Co-Creation**

The mobile internet is expanding what storytelling can do, bringing electronic games to portable, location-aware interfaces. This is the latest stage in a decades-long evolution of electronic games that aim to give players a fuller role, casting them as co-authors working alongside the original designers rather than mere avatars in a gameworld.

Location-aware interfaces let players pull places from the physical world into their gameworld, and vice versa. No other interactive media has done this before. Beyond giving players a role in worldmaking, mobile games abandon linear narratives in favor of cooperative storytelling that depends on the player's experience of place.

The idea of "author-player" worldmaking has existed before, yet mobile games push the process past the constraints of traditional video games. By extending worldmaking beyond the screen and into the physical world, location-aware interfaces turn the player's sensory experience of real places into storytelling tools.

In our essay, we theorize the unique storytelling potential of mobile games and describe our own attempt to realize it through the design and implementation of our hybrid-reality game, **University of Death**.
